Trying to Conceive

Basal Body Temperature: How to Chart BBT for Ovulation

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Basal body temperature, or BBT, is your body's lowest resting temperature, taken first thing in the morning before you get up, and it rises slightly after ovulation, so charting it each day can confirm that you ovulated. The catch is timing: the rise appears after the fertile window has mostly passed. That makes BBT a learning tool more than a same-day signal. This guide walks through the morning routine, how to read the chart, and what the numbers can honestly tell you.

What basal body temperature is and why it shifts

Basal body temperature is the lowest temperature your body reaches during rest. In the first part of a menstrual cycle, before ovulation, resting temperature sits in a lower band. After an egg is released, the follicle it came from starts producing progesterone, and progesterone nudges resting temperature upward. The rise is small, usually around 0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit, or about 0.3 to 0.6 degrees Celsius. You will not feel it, and a casual midday reading will not show it. The shift only becomes visible when you measure at the same quiet moment every morning and plot the numbers, day after day, on one chart.

That small rise is useful because of what causes it. Progesterone only climbs after ovulation, so a sustained temperature shift is reasonable evidence that an egg was released that cycle. This is the core of the method: BBT charting does not guess whether you might ovulate, it records whether you did. For someone who has been trying for a while, or whose cycles are unpredictable, that is valuable information on its own. A chart that shows a clear shift most months tells a calmer story than a stack of negative tests, and a chart that never shifts is worth showing to a clinician.

How to take your temperature

Take your temperature at the same time every morning, the moment you wake, before you sit up, talk, check your phone, or drink anything. Movement warms you quickly, and even a trip to the bathroom can blur the reading. You also need at least three to four hours of unbroken sleep beforehand, because short or broken sleep changes your resting temperature. Keep the thermometer on the nightstand within arm's reach the night before so the whole ritual takes under a minute. If your alarm time varies a lot, aim for the same window rather than perfection, and make a note on mornings that are far off schedule.

Use a basal thermometer, the kind that displays two decimal places. A standard fever thermometer rounds too coarsely to show a rise of half a degree reliably. Choose one route, oral is the most common, and use the same one all cycle, since readings from different sites do not compare well. Record the number immediately, because half-asleep memory is not dependable. Note anything unusual alongside it: a restless night, a late drink, illness, or travel. You can keep the chart on paper or log each reading in BeMama along with symptoms and questions for your next appointment. What matters is one consistent record in one place.

Reading the chart: the biphasic pattern

A full cycle of readings usually forms two levels, which is why charts are called biphasic. Temperatures sit in a lower band from your period until ovulation, then step up into a higher band and stay there until the next period begins. A common rule of thumb marks ovulation as the day before the first of three temperatures in a row that all sit clearly above the previous six days. Many charts draw a coverline just above that earlier band to make the shift easy to see. One high morning means little on its own. Look for a rise that holds for several days.

Do not worry much about the absolute numbers. Before ovulation, many people sit somewhere roughly between 97 and 98 degrees Fahrenheit, about 36.1 to 36.7 Celsius, but healthy baselines vary from person to person. The signal is the step up from your own lower band, not any particular value. After the rise, temperatures typically stay elevated until a day or two before your period, then drop. If a period does not arrive and temperatures stay up, that can be an early hint of pregnancy. Your chart also shows how many days sit between the rise and your period, which is your luteal phase, and our luteal phase guide covers how to read that length.

What BBT can and cannot tell you

Be clear-eyed about the method's core property: it confirms ovulation after the fact. By the time three high temperatures appear on the chart, the egg has already been released and the fertile window is mostly over. Sperm can wait up to about five days for an egg, but an egg lasts only about 12 to 24 hours, so acting on the rise itself is usually too late for that cycle. If you want advance warning instead, ovulation predictor kits detect the hormone surge before release, which is a different job and covered in our ovulation test guide. A thermometer looks backward; that is not a flaw, it is the design.

The real value shows up over two to three cycles. Charted patiently, your temperatures answer two questions that matter: does ovulation seem to be happening at all, and roughly when in your cycle does it tend to occur. Once you know that your shift usually lands around a certain cycle day, you can plan intercourse in future cycles ahead of that day rather than reacting to the chart. Many people pair charting with checking cervical mucus, which changes before ovulation and covers the forward-looking side, and our cervical mucus guide explains that method. Two or three real charts from your own body will teach you more about your cycle than any average table can.

Messy charts, confounders, and when to ask for help

Plenty of things can push a single morning's reading around: fever or any illness, alcohol the evening before, broken or short sleep, waking hours earlier or later than usual, travel across time zones, a much warmer bedroom, or some medicines. Shift work is the hardest case, because the method assumes one long sleep block; if your schedule rotates, take the reading after your longest sleep and expect a noisier chart. Do not delete odd readings. Circle them, note the reason, and read the overall trend instead. A chart with a few flagged mornings is still far more useful than no chart.

Bring your charts to a clinician if two or three careful cycles show no clear temperature shift, if your cycles are very irregular or unusually far apart, or if bleeding patterns have changed. It is also reasonable to book a fertility conversation after about a year of trying without success, or after about six months if you are 35 or older, whatever your charts look like. A flat chart does not prove you are not ovulating, since technique and sleep can hide the shift, but it is exactly the kind of pattern a clinician can help interpret. Real charts make that appointment more productive.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cycle length and ovulation timing vary, so calendar dates and home fertility signs provide estimates rather than proof. Temperature usually rises after ovulation, cervical mucus may change beforehand, and urine tests detect a hormone surge that suggests ovulation may follow.

Sleep disruption, illness, travel, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception, and irregular cycles can make patterns harder to interpret. Combining observations may provide useful context, but no home method confirms fertility or guarantees pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can place periods, temperatures, cervical mucus, symptoms, and test results on one timeline. Fertile-window dates are educational estimates and must not be used as contraception.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for persistently absent, very painful, unusually heavy, or highly irregular periods, or when a medical condition may affect fertility.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Fertility Awareness-Based Methods of Family Planning
  • ACOG — Evaluating Infertility

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Take your temperature at the same time every morning, before sitting up, after at least three to four hours of unbroken sleep.
  • Use a basal thermometer with two decimal places, because the rise after ovulation is only about 0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit.
  • Ovulation is usually marked by three temperatures in a row that sit clearly above the previous six days.
  • BBT confirms ovulation after the fact, so use two to three cycles of charts to learn your pattern, not to time sex that day.
  • Flag fever, alcohol, broken sleep, and travel on the chart, and show a persistently flat chart to a clinician.

Frequently asked questions

When should I take my basal body temperature?

Take it at the same time every morning, immediately after waking and before you sit up, talk, or get out of bed. You need at least three to four hours of unbroken sleep beforehand for the reading to reflect true rest. Consistency matters more than the exact hour, so pick a time you can repeat and note any morning that is far off schedule.

How much does BBT rise after ovulation?

Most people see a sustained rise of roughly 0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit, about 0.3 to 0.6 Celsius, in the day or two after ovulation. The rise is driven by progesterone from the follicle that released the egg. Because it is so small, you need a two-decimal basal thermometer, and you should wait for several high days in a row before reading anything into it.

Does BBT tell you when to have sex?

Not in the current cycle, because the temperature rise appears after ovulation, when the fertile window is already closing. Its value is confirming that you ovulate and showing which cycle day the shift usually lands on, so you can plan ahead in later cycles. For advance warning within a cycle, you need a sign that changes before ovulation, such as cervical mucus, which our cervical mucus guide covers.

What should my BBT be before ovulation?

Before ovulation, many people's readings sit somewhere roughly between 97 and 98 degrees Fahrenheit, about 36.1 to 36.7 Celsius, but healthy baselines vary. Your own consistent lower band is the reference that matters, because the method reads the shift above your baseline rather than any target number. If your baseline seems unusual to you, or your readings swing widely despite careful technique, mention it at your next appointment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
